title: Global epidemiology and genetic evolution of enterovirus D68 over a decade (2015-24): a systematic review.
abstract: Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a persistent global health concern, causing mild to severe respiratory disease and, in rare cases, acute flaccid myelitis, a polio-like paralytic syndrome. In this systematic review, we synthesised global data on the epidemiology and genetic evolution of EV-D68 from 2015 to 2024 and show its continued widespread circulation and concerning severity. 8184 EV-D68 cases were reported by 44 countries, and 267 (3·3%) of these cases were EV-D68-associated acute flaccid paralysis cases reported by 26 countries, across all continents. Biennial upsurges followed a distinct every-even-year pattern until 2020, after which the circulation showed geographical diversification in Europe and North America, possibly influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic. EV-D68 remained associated with severe respiratory disease and acute flaccid myelitis, not only primarily in children younger than five years but also increasingly in adults. Individuals who progressed to acute flaccid paralysis had poor prognosis for full recovery. Genotypic shifts were marked by the dominance of subgenotype B3 since 2016 and A2/D since 2018, with novel variants emerging for both after 2020. Despite limitations in surveillance quality and coverage, the findings underscore the need for sustained surveillance, improved diagnostic strategies, and targeted interventions to mitigate EV-D68-related morbidity.

title: Infection-specific long-chain fatty acid metabolism as a broad anti-enterovirus target
abstract: ABSTRACT Enteroviruses are arguably the most numerous group of viruses infecting humans. While most enterovirus infections are benign and self-resolving, their sheer number inevitably increases the chances of multiple complications. The diversity of enteroviruses means that the development of vaccines is only economically feasible against a select few, and no direct-acting or host-targeted anti-virals are approved to treat enteroviral infections, largely due to the rapid development of resistance against all experimental drugs. Here, we explored a universal property of enterovirus infection—a massive upregulation of phospholipid synthesis as a target for anti-viral interventions. The increased phospholipid synthesis consumes endogenously and exogenously derived long-chain fatty acids (LCFA). We demonstrate that polyunsaturated LCFAs can have a broad anti-enteroviral effect, affecting multiple steps of the virus life cycle. The anti-viral activity of LCFAs did not strictly depend on the degree of unsaturation or their capacity to induce lipid peroxidation, but significantly correlated with their conformation. This suggests that their incorporation into the phospholipid molecules makes the replication organelle membranes incapable of properly accommodating viral replication machinery. Accordingly, the inhibition of neutral lipid synthesis promoted LCFAs retargeting to the membranes in infected cells and increased their anti-viral potency. We show that this approach is effective against diverse enteroviruses in different cell types, including differentiated primary cells, and that attempts to establish viruses resistant to such treatment were unsuccessful. IMPORTANCE Humans are hosts to more than 300 distinct enteroviruses. Enterovirus infections can induce multiple short-term and long-term complications, including such serious conditions as paralysis, myocarditis, aseptic meningitis, and others. Yet, licensed vaccines are available only against poliovirus and enterovirus A71, and no specific anti-enterovirus drugs are approved for clinical practice. These viruses rapidly develop resistance to either virus- or host-acting experimental compounds. We explored a shared feature of enterovirus infection, a strong upregulation of phospholipid synthesis in infected cells, as a tool to control enterovirus replication. By altering the long-chain fatty acids composition available to infected cells, replication of diverse enteroviruses can be similarly suppressed, and the selection of resistant mutants was not successful. Thus, targeting infection-induced changes in cellular lipid metabolism, rather than individual viral or host factors, may offer a promising approach for controlling enterovirus infections.

source_records.abstract: ABSTRACT Enteroviruses are arguably the most numerous group of viruses infecting humans. While most enterovirus infections are benign and self-resolving, their sheer number inevitably increases the chances of multiple complications. The diversity of enteroviruses means that the development of vaccines is only economically feasible against a select few, and no direct-acting or host-targeted anti-virals are approved to treat enteroviral infections, largely due to the rapid development of resistance against all experimental drugs. Here, we explored a universal property of enterovirus infection—a massive upregulation of phospholipid synthesis as a target for anti-viral interventions. The increased phospholipid synthesis consumes endogenously and exogenously derived long-chain fatty acids (LCFA). We demonstrate that polyunsaturated LCFAs can have a broad anti-enteroviral effect, affecting multiple steps of the virus life cycle. The anti-viral activity of LCFAs did not strictly depend on the degree of unsaturation or their capacity to induce lipid peroxidation, but significantly correlated with their conformation. This suggests that their incorporation into the phospholipid molecules makes the replication organelle membranes incapable of properly accommodating viral replication machinery. Accordingly, the inhibition of neutral lipid synthesis promoted LCFAs retargeting to the membranes in infected cells and increased their anti-viral potency. title: Surveillance bias and the hidden ecology of Enterovirus coxsackiepol: implications for global risk assessment of vaccine-derived poliovirus emergence.
abstract: Abstract Global enterovirus (EV) surveillance has long relied on RD/L20B cell culture systems optimized for poliovirus (PV) detection. This systematically under-detected Enterovirus coxsackiepol (EV-C) while over-representing Enterovirus betacoxsackie (EV-B). This bias created a fundamental paradox: circulating vaccine-derived polioviruses (cVDPVs), including those of novel oral polio vaccine type 2 origin, have genomic regions of non-polio EV-C origin, suggesting frequent recombination with viruses rarely detected in surveillance datasets. Here, we show that EV-C viruses might be more prevalent and widely distributed than recognized. We further show that regions considered low risk for cVDPV emergence (especially those using only inactivated PV vaccine and acute flaccid paralysis surveillance) may harbor undetected non-polio EV-C circulation and silent PV transmission. We propose integrating wastewater (WW) surveillance, long-range reverse transcription-PCR (amplifying the complete or coding-complete genome as a single contig), and long-read sequencing to capture full EV diversity, improve cVDPV emergence risk assessment, and strengthen PV-eradication efforts. Expanding this framework to other viruses can facilitate the 100-day mission by enabling the acquisition of actionable intelligence for all such viruses directly from WW. Furthermore, this creates an opportunity to harmonize PV surveillance with broader pandemic preparedness frameworks, allowing investments in PV genomic surveillance to generate cross-pathogen benefits.

title: Development of Therapeutics for Orthopoxvirus and Enterovirus infections: Small Molecule Antiviral Drug Discovery and Library Generation
abstract: Endemic diseases have the potential to spread quickly and overwhelm vulnerable populations, leading to the necessity for antiviral drugs to treat infections. This work focuses on the development of antivirals for orthopoxviruses and enteroviruses, as well as compound library development. Orthopoxviruses, which include monkeypox virus (mpox), vaccinia virus, and the eradicated smallpox virus, have few approved therapies, with no antiviral drug being approved for mpox infection. The viral p37 protein is a known therapeutic target for poxvirus antivirals. Tecovirimat is a known p37 inhibitor; however, it did not effectively treat mpox infections in clinical trials. Tecovirimat contains a large hydrocarbon motif, and previous changes in this motif have retained some antiviral efficacy. We identified a series of compounds containing amide, hydrazide, and carbamide linkers with adamantane, noradamantane, and other cyclic hydrocarbon substitutions with sub-micromolar potency targeting p37. The second focus of this work was the development of antivirals targeting Enterovirus-D68 (EV-D68). EV-D68 is an upper respiratory virus associated with polio-like acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) and primarily represents a threat to children under 16. Currently, there is no vaccine or Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug to combat EV-D68 infections. We used high-throughput screening to identify a promising hit molecule that we further optimized. We identified that the target was the VP1 capsid protein. We identified candidates Jun14135 and Jun14934 having broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple strains of EV-D68. Furthermore, we identified the potential for co-therapy opportunities of Jun16934 with the EV-D68 2C inhibitor Jun6504. Finally, we look to improve the speed of preclinical development for covalent inhibitors by developing a direct-to-biology (D2B) methodology to quickly synthesize molecules for screening. D2B is being increasingly utilized by both industry and academia, primarily due to the potential to save both time and cost by using small amounts of crude reactions for use in biological assays.

title_zh: 正痘病毒和肠道病毒感染疗法的开发:小分子 抗病毒药物 药物发现和文库生成
source_body_en: Endemic diseases have the potential to spread quickly and overwhelm vulnerable populations, leading to the necessity for antiviral drugs to treat infections. This work focuses on the development of antivirals for orthopoxviruses and enteroviruses, as well as compound library development. Orthopoxviruses, which include monkeypox virus (mpox), vaccinia virus, and the eradicated smallpox virus, have few approved therapies, with no antiviral drug being approved for mpox infection. The viral p37 protein is a known therapeutic target for poxvirus antivirals. Tecovirimat is a known p37 inhibitor; however, it did not effectively treat mpox infections in clinical trials. Tecovirimat contains a large hydrocarbon motif, and previous changes in this motif have retained some antiviral efficacy. We identified a series of compounds containing amide, hydrazide, and carbamide linkers with adamantane, noradamantane, and other cyclic hydrocarbon substitutions with sub-micromolar potency targeting p37. The second focus of this work was the development of antivirals targeting Enterovirus-D68 (EV-D68). EV-D68 is an upper respiratory virus associated with polio-like acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) and primarily represents a threat to children under 16. Currently, there is no vaccine or Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved drug to combat EV-D68 infections. We used high-throughput screening to identify a promising hit molecule that we further optimized. We identified that the target was the VP1 capsid protein. We identified candidates Jun14135 and Jun14934 having broad-spectrum antiviral activity against multiple strains of EV-D68. Furthermore, we identified the potential for co-therapy opportunities of Jun16934 with the EV-D68 2C inhibitor Jun6504. Finally, we look to improve the speed of preclinical development for covalent inhibitors by developing a direct-to-biology (D2B) methodology to quickly synthesize molecules for screening. D2B is being increasingly utilized by both industry and academia, primarily due to the potential to save both time and cost by using small amounts of crude reactions for use in biological assays.
